clue.text: Large packing-case a girl takes to Georgia

parts.note: Sara is a girl's name
taken as written
GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia

explanation.surface: Someone sends a big crate off to a girl living in Georgia.
explanation.walkthrough: A Saratoga trunk is a large travelling trunk, named after the American spa town.
explanation.definitionFit: A Saratoga is a big domed travelling trunk of the nineteenth century, a crate-like piece of luggage.

clue.text: Seems a sort of oil-producing plant

indicators.note: a sort of something is a version of it, so these letters are formed into a new version

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that something looks like a kind of oil plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' tells you to rearrange SEEMS and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Sesame seeds are pressed to give a cooking oil, so the plant is grown for its oil.

clue.text: The disturbance behind us

parts.note: the behind is the rump, the backside
taken as written

explanation.surface: A commotion is going on just behind where we stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' looks like a position word but is a noun for the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumpus is a noisy uproar or commotion.

clue.text: Tales lacking point for right minded people

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so a letter is removed from the word for tales

parts.note: tales are stories
S, for south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Stories without a moral point told for the benefit of the right-thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right minded' is a pun: Tories are on the political right.
explanation.definitionFit: Tories are Conservatives, people whose politics lean to the right.

clue.text: A building of growing concern .

parts.note: a glass building used for raising plants, where growing is the concern; also a nod to the 'growing concern' over the climate effect named after it

explanation.surface: A firm's headquarters described as a growing concern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'growing concern' usually means a thriving business, but here the concern is literally growing plants.
explanation.definitionFit: A glasshouse is a building in which gardeners grow plants under glass.

clue.text: First celebrated by the Red Queen?

definitions.text: First celebrated by the Red Queen?

parts.words: First celebrated by the Red Queen
parts.note: the first of a spring month, kept as a workers' festival by communists (Reds) and with a Queen of the May at village festivities

explanation.surface: A character from Alice is throwing her first party.
explanation.walkthrough: The Red Queen is from Through the Looking-Glass, but here 'Red' means communist: 1 May is the workers' holiday, and a May Queen is crowned on that day.
explanation.definitionFit: The first day of the fifth month is a spring festival and international labour day.

clue.text: … going up on a North American footing

parts.note: a footing is a basis or foundation

explanation.surface: A rise in fortunes now set on a North American base.
explanation.walkthrough: Anabasis is Greek for a march up-country, the title of Xenophon's history; 'on' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: Anabasis means an ascent or advance inland, literally a march upward.

clue.text: Man on board who shows the way

explanation.surface: A board member who leads the way.
explanation.definitionFit: A company director sits on the board of management, and a director also guides others, showing them where to go.

clue.text: Vocalist who scales the heights

parts.note: an Alpine singer who runs up and down musical scales, and whose home is the mountain heights

explanation.surface: A singer who climbs mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scales' means both climbing and running up and down musical scales, as Alpine singing leaps between registers.
explanation.definitionFit: This kind of singer warbles with rapid switches between chest voice and falsetto, a tradition of Swiss mountain herders.

clue.text: Where several start and rest follow haphazardly

parts.note: several is a vague quantity, like some

indicators.note: haphazardly means in random order, so the letters of rest are jumbled

explanation.surface: Instructions for a race where several start and the rest follow in a disorderly bunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start' and 'follow' fix the order of the two parts. SOMERSET is a county in south-west England; 'Where' is the definition because a county is a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset is an English county, a place, so it answers the question of location.

clue.text: Not allowed, except one colour

parts.note: bar can mean except, as in 'all bar one'
red is one colour

explanation.surface: Every colour is permitted except one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'except' is the preposition 'bar', as in 'bar none'.
explanation.definitionFit: If something is barred it is prohibited or forbidden.

clue.text: Avenue I'm exploring for a purple dye

indicators.note: exploring suggests moving about, so the letters of avenue and I'm wander into a new order

parts.note: the apostrophe is not a letter

explanation.surface: Wandering down an avenue in search of a purple dye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exploring' tells you to rearrange AVENUE and IM.
explanation.definitionFit: Mauveine, made by Perkin in 1856, was the first synthetic aniline dye, a mauve colour.

clue.text: French a philosopher friend embracing little science

indicators.note: embracing means holding round, so the word for friend surrounds the other letters

parts.note: a pal is a friend
SC is a short form of science

explanation.surface: A French thinker hugging a friend who has a little scientific knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: PAL holds A and SC.
explanation.definitionFit: Blaise Pascal was a seventeenth-century French mathematician and religious thinker.

clue.text: One of a number in the bar recognised in half a shake

definitions.text: One of a number in the bar

parts.note: semi- is a prefix meaning half
a quaver is a trill or tremble, a shake in the voice

explanation.surface: Someone among a crowd in a pub is recognised almost instantly.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bar' is a bar of music and the 'number' of notes in it, not a pub. 'in half a shake' plays on the phrase 'in half a mo'.
explanation.definitionFit: A semiquaver is a sixteenth note, one of several notes that make up a musical bar.

clue.text: Had a stroke of luck on the golf course

definitions.text: Had a stroke of luck on the golf course

parts.words: Had a stroke of luck on the golf course
parts.note: on a golf course, one lucky stroke sends the ball straight from the tee into the cup

explanation.surface: A golfer enjoyed some good fortune during a round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stroke' means a golf shot, and the luck is to need only one for the hole.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer who sinks the ball with the first shot from the tee has made an ace.

clue.text: A look at television in profile?

definitions.text: A look at television in profile?

parts.words: A look at television in profile
parts.note: a glance at a set from the edge, seen sideways, a picture in profile

explanation.surface: A survey of the television industry presented as a profile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'profile' means a magazine portrait, but here it is the outline seen from the edge; 'side' was also slang for a TV channel.
explanation.definitionFit: A view from the side shows a thing in profile, its outline seen edgeways.

clue.text: Food concocted for me in Laos

indicators.note: concocted means cooked up, so the letters of me, in and Laos are mixed into new food

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dish cooked up for the speaker while in Laos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concocted' tells you to rearrange ME, IN and LAOS.
explanation.definitionFit: Semolina is coarse durum wheat flour used for puddings and pasta.

clue.text: Hot stuff from Jamaica — quite risqué!

definitions.text: Hot stuff from Jamaica — quite risqué!

parts.words: Hot stuff from Jamaica — quite risqué
parts.note: a pungent Caribbean berry, also called Jamaica pepper, whose name suggests 'all spicy', that is quite risqué

explanation.surface: A racy performer from Jamaica described as hot stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot stuff' suggests a sexy person, and 'quite risqué' is 'all spicy'; really it is a spice.
explanation.definitionFit: This spice is the dried berry of a Caribbean tree, also known as Jamaica pepper or pimento.

clue.text: Impracticable, perhaps, in italicised form

indicators.note: putting the word into another form means shaping its letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A dreamy idea set out in sloping type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in ... form' tells you to rearrange ITALICISED; 'perhaps' marks the definition as an example of the answer's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Lofty principles may be too visionary to put into practice, hence unrealistic.

clue.text: Wins points for musical arrangements

explanation.surface: A musician earns credit for orchestrations.
explanation.definitionFit: A team scores when it gains points, and composers write scores, the full written versions of pieces for performers.

clue.text: Elementary meal prepared to give inside information

definitions.text: Elementary meal prepared to give inside information

parts.words: Elementary meal prepared to give inside information
parts.note: a chemical-element drink swallowed before an X-ray so that the gut shows up, revealing what is going on inside

explanation.surface: A simple dinner cooked to loosen someone's tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside information' usually means secrets, but here it is an X-ray picture of the stomach; 'Elementary' points to a chemical element.
explanation.definitionFit: This element, number 56, is given as a sulphate 'meal' to outline the digestive tract in X-rays.

clue.text: Flag for a leading Quaker getting on

parts.note: William Penn was a leading Quaker who founded Pennsylvania
taken as written

explanation.surface: A banner for a prominent Quaker who is getting on in years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' just links the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A pennon is a long narrow pennant flown from a lance or masthead.

clue.text: Selfish person for example put own entrance first

definitions.text: Selfish person for example put own entrance first

parts.words: Selfish person for example put own entrance first
parts.note: someone self-centred barging in, putting their own arrival ahead of everyone else's

explanation.surface: A selfish type insists on making their entrance before anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes the conduct of someone wholly self-centred.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a person thinks chiefly of self and their own interests.

clue.text: Pay for tea in a little bag

indicators.note: in tells you the tea goes inside the bag

parts.note: a purse is a small bag for money
cha (char) is a British slang word for tea

explanation.surface: Settling the bill for tea kept in a small bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pay for' is a verb phrase meaning buy, matching the verb sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To purchase something is to buy it, handing over money.

clue.text: Complaint from flower-girl getting it in the eye

indicators.note: getting here means receiving, so the girl takes the word it inside her name

parts.note: Iris is both a flower and a girl's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flower-seller is hit in the eye by something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' signals the container; 'in the eye' points to where the complaint is, as the iris is part of the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Iritis is an inflammation of the coloured ring of the eye, a medical disorder.

clue.text: Dislike of an interpretation

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, a
a version is one interpretation of events

explanation.surface: Someone disliking a particular reading of a text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An aversion is a strong dislike or antipathy.

clue.text: Bottom was one, we swear

parts.note: taken as written
to aver is to declare or swear

explanation.surface: A claim about someone's backside sworn to by witnesses.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottom is the weaver in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, not a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick Bottom works at a loom in Shakespeare's comedy, making cloth.

clue.text: Presumably they haven't had time to get tired of college life

definitions.text: Presumably they haven't had time to get tired of college life

parts.words: Presumably they haven't had time to get tired of college life
parts.note: first-year students, newly arrived, are still unjaded by university

explanation.surface: Musings on students not yet weary of campus.
explanation.walkthrough: The pun is on 'fresh' as opposed to tired.
explanation.definitionFit: First-year undergraduates have only just begun university, so they are new to it.
